title: Latin Doesn't Make Surgeons: Exams Should Be Hard at Something Useful
dek: Latin doesn't make surgeons: skills barely transfer. If you assume "the harder the subject, the sharper the mind," a nation's brightest get wasted on the most useless knowledge — that is the lesson of the Qing examination system.
why: It puts imperial civil-service exams, military selection and modern transfer experiments on a single chain of evidence, unusually connecting history with talent assessment — and the two sides genuinely clash.
who: Gatekeepers of talent assessment, exam design, school curricula and civil-service hiring, plus every teacher, parent and learner who believes "a hard subject sharpens the mind."
skip: The first stretch of Qing examination history is slow; if you're short on time, start at 22:51 with the British civil-service reform.

points.h: Wrong exam content dooms a nation even with brilliant candidates
points.body: Hong Xiuquan failed the Qing examinations at least four times. After the last failure, he had visions on the road home, believed himself the younger brother of Christ, and eventually launched the Taiping Rebellion — which Daisy says may be the deadliest civil war in human history, with deaths around thirty million. He was not alone: examination seats were far fewer than the number of candidates, many sat into their forties and fifties without passing, and the only way home was to teach. Daisy adds that the deeper cost fell on those who did pass: they mastered the eight-legged essay while knowing nothing of the science and mathematics transforming the world. When the brightest young men can only practise a dead format, the country bleeds from both directions at once.

points.h: British civil-service reform was elites reproducing themselves
points.body: The Northcote-Trevelyan Report is often seen by the British as the founding document of the modern civil service, but Daisy backs the revisionist judgment: under the banner of a unified exam, it pushed Oxford and Cambridge classics graduates into key posts. Benjamin Jowett, master of Balliol, worked behind the scenes to place his classics students throughout the empire. Michael Coolican's "No Tradesmen and No Women" points out that the 1854 report reduced the most naked buying and selling of offices, but also snuffed out the professional exams that were already growing in various departments. It is not that exams cannot select people — it is what they examine that decides whether they select the able or select people like oneself.

points.h: A bureaucracy without price signals corrects itself through corpses
points.body: Daisy attributes bureaucratic failure to the absence of feedback: no price mechanism, no profit and loss, so a department cannot tell whether its plans save or kill. The military sounds like a counterexample, but military bureaucracies err just as constantly in peacetime; almost every time Britain went to war after a long peace, a crisis brewed in the first year, as with the shell crisis at the start of World War I. What actually forces correction then is not internal inspection but mass death on the battlefield. She calls it a correction mechanism crueler than prices. To make a bureaucracy reliable, you first have to create a signal that shows consequences; otherwise no amount of rigor in selection can save the quality of everyday decisions.

points.h: The Royal Navy won by examining navigation, not Latin
points.body: Daisy notes that the real pillar of Victorian Britain was not the army but the Royal Navy. As early as 1677, after the navy kept losing to the Dutch, Samuel Pepys set up an oral exam for captains: three senior officers questioned them face to face on how to command a ship. Over the following century, navigation, charting and trigonometry entered the written exams, and chart-makers like Nelson, Cook, Flinders and Bligh all passed through this gate. Daisy uses this to draw out two exam traditions: Pepys tested skills needed immediately; Macaulay and Northcote-Trevelyan later wanted to test classical languages. One served navigational safety, the other served a caste barrier, and the results naturally differed.

points.h: Content doesn't matter? Macaulay's screening argument misses a key link
points.body: Here comes the highlight: Daisy reads aloud Macaulay's 1833 parliamentary speech. The gist is that whatever a age happens to teach, the best at it will necessarily be the cleverest, most industrious and most honor-seeking of the young; so Cambridge could teach Ptolemy instead of Newton and its top students would still be excellent; teach Cherokee instead of Greek and the best Cherokee scholar would still be a great man; even astrology and alchemy would do. Another MP immediately praised it as the most practically wise speech in parliamentary history, but Daisy says flatly: this is more like being carried away by one's own eloquence, and it completely misses that "what you learn really does matter."

points.h: Dead twigs and corn: wrong content makes discipline just watering
points.body: Daisy closes out Macaulay with the 1917 rebuttal of the American medical educator Abraham Flexner. Flexner said the devotees of mental training are like Egyptian priests: they stick a row of dead twigs in the soil and then water them on schedule for the sake of discipline. Plant corn and the discipline is no less, with a crop thrown in. Against the American medical schools of the day, where many aspiring doctors were forced to study Greek and Latin before touching a medical book, Flexner's answer was: medicine is already hard enough, and using it to sharpen the mind is far more efficient than using dead languages. Daisy agrees: spend the best years of the most gifted on what has been disproved or is useless, and the only winner is the rival who has its young learn real knowledge.

points.h: Rectangles don't train triangles: transfer needs identical elements
points.body: Thorndike designed a cleaner controlled experiment: have people repeatedly estimate the area of rectangles until they clearly improve, then have them estimate the area of triangles — almost no transfer. If even two shapes this close show nothing, the claim that "classical languages sharpen the mind" is even less credible. Thorndike's explanation was identical elements: transfer appears only when old and new tasks share the same components; far transfer essentially breaks down. Daisy draws the exam-design principle from this: to select people who can navigate, test navigation and trigonometry; to select people who can practise medicine, test medicine. A genuinely effective exam attaches difficulty directly to the real task.
